domain_entities.name: PortEnvironmentInput
attributes: rawValue: string | undefined — the exact value of process.env.PORT as observed; undefined when the variable is not present in the environment
presence: PortPresence — ABSENT | PRESENT, derived from whether rawValue is undefined
observedAt: Date — the instant the snapshot was taken (process bootstrap)
domain_entities.purpose: The immutable snapshot of the process environment's PORT entry, taken once at startup. It is the sole input to port resolution and exists to make the three observable cases (unset / valid / invalid) explicit domain states rather than an implicit `string | undefined`.
lifecycle_states: ABSENT — PORT is not present in the environment (rawValue === undefined). Resolution must select the default port.

PRESENT — PORT is present as a string, which may be empty, whitespace-only, non-numeric, zero, negative, fractional, or a valid positive integer. Resolution must classify it via the canonical validity predicate.
No transitions: the snapshot is taken once and never mutated. ABSENT and PRESENT are terminal observations, not a progression.

domain_entities.name: ResolvedHttpPort
attributes: port: number — the effective TCP port; always a positive integer (1..65535) by construction
source: PortSource — ENV | DEFAULT, recording which branch produced the value
rawValue: string | undefined — the originating PORT string, retained for diagnostics only; never logged verbatim if it could be non-numeric garbage (see GP-004 note in domainNotes)
domain_entities.purpose: The single authoritative port value the process will bind to, produced by resolving a PortEnvironmentInput. It is the only value permitted to reach the listen call and the startup log line, so the two can never disagree.
lifecycle_states: RESOLVED — the port has been derived from the environment snapshot and is ready to be bound. This is the only state; resolution is a pure, total function from PortEnvironmentInput to ResolvedHttpPort, so there is no failure state and no transition.
BOUND — the resolved port has been handed to the HTTP listener and the listener accepted it. Reached only from RESOLVED, exactly once per process.
LISTEN_FAILED — the listener rejected the bind (e.g. the port is already in use). Reached only from RESOLVED; terminal for the process (existing behaviour: log the error and exit non-zero).
No transition from BOUND back to RESOLVED: the port is resolved once at bootstrap and is not re-read or re-resolved while the process runs.

business_rules: The HTTP port is supplied by exactly one source: the PORT environment variable, resolved once at process bootstrap. No literal port number may be passed to the HTTP listener anywhere else in the codebase, and no other environment variable may override or supplement PORT. The name is matched exactly and case-sensitively (PORT, not port/Port). [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever HTTP port configuration (every site that supplies or consumes the listen port) appears, not only here]

Canonical port validity predicate — a PORT value is VALID if and only if it is a non-empty string that, after trimming leading/trailing whitespace, matches /^[0-9]+$/ (ASCII digits only, no sign, no decimal point, no exponent, no thousands separator, no surrounding text) AND whose numeric value is >= 1 AND <= 65535. Every other value is INVALID. This single predicate is the only definition of validity; no call site may apply a looser or stricter test (e.g. parseInt alone, Number() alone, or a bare truthiness check). [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever PORT validity classification (every site that decides whether a PORT value is usable) appears, not only here]

Fallback rule — when PORT is ABSENT, or PRESENT but INVALID under the canonical validity predicate, the resolved port is the default 3000 with source DEFAULT. The fallback is silent: it never throws, never aborts startup, and never emits a warning or error. A malformed PORT therefore degrades to the default rather than failing the process. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever HTTP port resolution (default selection) appears, not only here]

Single-resolution / single-source-of-truth rule — the port is resolved exactly once per process, and the resulting ResolvedHttpPort.port is the ONLY value used for both the listen call and the startup log line. The log line must report the port actually bound, so it can never disagree with the listener; re-reading process.env.PORT at log time (or anywhere after resolution) is forbidden. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever HTTP port resolution and startup logging (every consumer of the resolved port) appears, not only here]

Resolution is a pure, total function of the environment snapshot: resolvePort(input: PortEnvironmentInput) -> ResolvedHttpPort. It performs no I/O, reads no global state other than the snapshot it is given, and has no failure mode — every input maps to exactly one output. It must be callable in a unit test without starting a server, binding a socket, or mutating process.env. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever HTTP port resolution (testability and determinism of the resolver) appears, not only here]

The resolved port is a positive integer in the range 1..65535 inclusive. Zero, negative values, fractional values, and values above 65535 are INVALID and fall back to 3000. Port 0 (OS-assigned ephemeral port) is deliberately NOT honoured via PORT, because the startup log line must report a concrete port; tests that need an ephemeral port bind port 0 directly through the Fastify instance (the existing scripts/smoke.js pattern) rather than through PORT. [BINDING RULE — apply this wherever PORT validity classification (numeric range boundary) appears, not only here]

The startup log line keeps its existing exact shape and wording — `Server is running on http://localhost:${port}` — with the resolved port interpolated. The host in the message stays the literal `localhost` even though the listener binds host 0.0.0.0; the message is a developer convenience, not a statement of the bind address, and this feature does not change it.

The raw PORT string is never logged, echoed in an error message, or returned in any response. Only the resolved numeric port (and, at most, the PortSource classification) may appear in logs. This keeps a malformed or hostile environment value out of the log stream (GP-004).

Port resolution is a bootstrap concern only and is not a state-changing domain operation: it writes no audit record (GP-002 does not apply), requires no authentication or role check (GP-005 does not apply), and opens no transaction. It must not be routed through the repository layer (GP-001 does not apply — there is no persisted entity).
domain_notes:
## Scope of this domain slice

This feature has **no persisted domain entity**. It introduces a bootstrap/process-configuration concern into the composition root (`src/index.ts`), which currently hardcodes `const PORT = 3000`. The domain slice is therefore two value objects and a pure resolution function, not a table-backed aggregate. No new tables, no repository, no migration, no audit record, no RBAC, no transaction — see the golden-principle applicability rule.

## Lifecycle states introduced (for architectureMdUpdate)

Every state below must be folded into the architecture document. None of them are persisted; all are in-process bootstrap states.

**PortEnvironmentInput**
- `ABSENT` — PORT not present in the environment (`rawValue === undefined`).
- `PRESENT` — PORT present as a string (may be empty, whitespace, non-numeric, zero, negative, fractional, or a valid positive integer).
- No transitions: the snapshot is taken once at bootstrap and never mutated. Both states are terminal observations.

**ResolvedHttpPort**
- `RESOLVED` — the port has been derived from the snapshot; the only entry state.
- `BOUND` — the resolved port was handed to the HTTP listener and accepted. Reached only from `RESOLVED`, exactly once per process.
- `LISTEN_FAILED` — the listener rejected the bind (e.g. port in use). Reached only from `RESOLVED`; terminal for the process (existing behaviour: log the error, exit non-zero).
- No transition from `BOUND` back to `RESOLVED`: the port is resolved once and never re-read.

## Relationship to the existing architecture

- **Extends, does not contradict.** The existing architecture has no configuration module; the only `process.env` reads are inline (`DATABASE_URL` in `src/shared/db/connection.ts`, `JWT_SECRET` in `src/shared/auth/index.ts`). This feature adds a third inline read unless the open question about a `src/shared/config/` module is resolved otherwise. That question is surfaced, not silently decided.
- **No module boundary is created by this slice.** Whether one should be is open question #1; the application architect owns the answer.
- **`scripts/smoke.js` is unaffected** — it binds `port: 0` directly on the Fastify instance and never goes through `src/index.ts`, so it neither reads nor is affected by PORT. This is why port 0 is deliberately excluded from the valid range: the ephemeral-port test path already exists and does not need PORT.
- **No existing lifecycle state changes.** Employee, LeaveType, LeavePolicy, LeaveRequest, LeaveBalance, AuditLog and Notification lifecycles are untouched.

## Binding decisions made here (broad scope, applies everywhere)

1. PORT is the single source of the listen port; no literal port anywhere else.
2. One canonical validity predicate (digits-only after trim, 1..65535) — no call site may apply a looser test.
3. Invalid or absent → 3000, silently, never throwing.
4. Resolve once; the resolved value feeds both the listener and the log line, so they cannot disagree.
5. Resolution is a pure total function, unit-testable without a socket or `process.env` mutation.
6. Port 0 is invalid via PORT (the log line must report a concrete port).
7. The raw PORT string is never logged (GP-004).

## Concerns to surface to the chief architect

- **The feature text is under-specified at exactly the boundary its third test case probes.** "Not a positive integer" reads as strict, but the idiomatic Node implementation (`parseInt`) is lenient and would accept `'3000abc'` as 3000. I recorded the strict predicate as the binding rule and raised the choice as open question #2 rather than leaving the lenient behaviour implicit at one call site — this is the BR-001 anti-pattern the task warns about, and the same predicate governs both the fallback decision and the value actually bound.
- **Silent fallback is an operability risk.** A typo'd PORT in a deployment manifest becomes invisible and the service quietly binds 3000 — the exact collision this feature exists to prevent. Recorded as open question #3.
- **The architecture document's "Open questions" list already carries unrelated items** (day-count calendar vs business days, accrual model, carry-forward cap, migration mechanism, controller layer, BullMQ). The three questions raised here are new and distinct; do not merge them into that list without labelling them as this feature's.
- **No golden principle is engaged by this feature.** GP-001 (no repository), GP-002 (no state change), GP-005 (no endpoint) do not apply; GP-004 applies only as the "never log the raw PORT string" rule. If a reviewer expects an audit record for the port change, that expectation is wrong — nothing is persisted.

open_questions.question: Where does port resolution live: inline in src/index.ts (matching the existing inline process.env reads in shared/db/connection.ts and shared/auth/index.ts), or in a new shared configuration module (e.g. src/shared/config/) that becomes the single home for all environment reads?
open_questions.impact: Determines whether "process configuration" becomes a first-class domain concept with its own module boundary, or stays a bootstrap detail. The architecture currently has NO configuration module and three ad-hoc inline env reads (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET, and now PORT); choosing inline perpetuates that, choosing a module creates a new shared boundary that the other two reads arguably belong in. Affects the application architect's module map and the dependency rules.
candidate_options: Inline in src/index.ts — smallest diff, matches existing precedent, no new module boundary
New src/shared/config/ module owning PORT resolution now, with DATABASE_URL/JWT_SECRET migration deferred
New src/shared/config/ module owning PORT resolution now AND migrating the two existing env reads in the same feature

open_questions.question: Should the canonical port validity predicate be strict (digits-only regex, so '3000abc', '3e3', ' 3000 ' and '0xBB8' are all INVALID and fall back to 3000) or lenient (parseInt/Number coercion, so '3000abc' resolves to 3000)?
open_questions.impact: This is the boundary the feature's third test case sits on. The feature text says "not a positive integer" falls back to 3000, which reads as strict, but the common Node idiom (parseInt) is lenient and would silently accept '3000abc' as 3000. The two choices disagree on a whole class of inputs and the choice must be made once for the predicate, not per call site.
candidate_options: Strict: trim, then require /^[0-9]+$/ and 1 <= n <= 65535; anything else falls back to 3000 (recommended — matches 'not a positive integer')
Lenient: Number.parseInt(value, 10) and accept when the result is a positive integer, so '3000abc' -> 3000
Strict digits-only but with no upper bound (accept 70000 and let the listener fail)

open_questions.question: When PORT is present but invalid, should the fallback be completely silent, or should the process emit a warning naming the offending value?
open_questions.impact: Affects operability: a silent fallback means a typo'd PORT in a deployment manifest is invisible and the service quietly binds 3000, which is exactly the collision this feature exists to prevent. A warning improves diagnosis but risks logging an arbitrary environment string (GP-004 tension). The feature text specifies only the fallback value, not the observability of the fallback.
candidate_options: Silent fallback — no log, no warning (simplest; matches the feature text literally)
Warn via app.log.warn with the PortSource classification only, never the raw string
Warn including the raw value — rejected by the GP-004 rule above unless explicitly overridden

open_questions.question: Should the resolved port be exposed as a testable seam (e.g. an exported resolvePort function or a fastify.port decoration) so the unit test exercises the resolver directly, or should the test drive src/index.ts as a module and assert on the listen call?
open_questions.impact: Determines whether the required unit test is a pure function test (fast, no socket, no process.env mutation) or an integration-style test that must mock app.listen and re-import the entry point per case. The feature mandates three cases (unset, valid, non-numeric) but does not say at which seam they are asserted; the choice also decides whether src/index.ts stays a side-effecting script or gains an exported pure function.
candidate_options: Export a pure resolvePort(input) from the entry point (or a config module) and unit-test it directly with three cases
Keep resolution inline and test by mocking app.listen + jest.resetModules + process.env manipulation per case
Both: pure resolver unit test plus one entry-point wiring test asserting the log line matches the bound port
